title: latency-driven-traffic-diversion-playbook-draft
content:
TL;DR:
This is a working draft runbook for latency-driven cross-region diversion (we call it "LD-TrafficDiv"). It documents detection, quick mitigation, and controlled cutover steps when an entire region shows sustained latency or partial network flakiness. Focus is on: minimizing user-perceived error/latency, preserving KV cache locality where possible, and ensuring fast rollback.

Context / motivation:
- We operate in 3 active regions + 1 warm-standby. Certain failure modes (regional upstream peering issues, degenerate load balancer behavior, or regional control plane interruptions) present as spike in P50/P95 token-latency and/or increased 5xx across frontends for a subset of POPs.
- Full manual DNS failover is blunt and slow; BGP/anycast changes are faster but require NOC coordination and have broader blast radius. This playbook provides an operator-friendly, latency-first set of options that start with narrow traffic diversion (weights / latency steering) and escalate to warm-standby promotion only when necessary.

Acceptance criteria for use:
- Alert: regional_latency_spike OR regional_request_error_rate > 3x baseline for > 5 minutes
- Observability: corroborating traces show requests successfully reaching backends but latency backend-side is fast (indicates network hop issue) OR errors originate at edge (indicates LB/NGINX problem).
- Communication: paging for P1 and notify CS/Platform channel.

Quick mitigation (first 8 minutes):
1) Confirm scope: run 'dig +short @8.8.8.8 redwood.example.com' from multiple regions (cloud shell + dev machine) and compare TTLs and results. Run traceroute to failing region from both a healthy region and an external vantage point.
2) If DNS resolution inconsistent -> check Route53 / Cloud DNS health and pending changes. Confirm no recent change-batch authored in last 10 mins.
3) If traffic hits edge but errors: change upstream health-check thresholds in LB to more forgiving values for 2 minutes to avoid transient 5xx cascades.
4) Temporarily reduce new connection rate: increase rate-limiter bucket at API gateway for the affected region by -20% to reduce cascading backpressure.

Decision matrix (narrow to wide):
- If only some POPs / subset of customers affected and latency is < 2x baseline: prefer weight adjustments and latency-steering.
- If region-wide SLO degradation (> 25% user impact) or BGP/peering blackholing suspected: escalate to warm-standby promotion.

Weight-adjustment / latency-steering steps (safe, reversible):
1) In Traffic Director / Global LB, reduce weight of affected region by 20-40% and proportionally increase healthy regions. Observe for 2 minutes.
2) If provider supports latency-rt steering (eg: geo-latency-target): create a temporary policy to prefer healthy region for specific routes (chat/generation endpoints) only.
3) Update CDN origin failover rules if fronted by our CDN (purge or change origin weights).
Commands / examples:
- Route53 weight change (example):
  aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 --change-batch '{
    "Changes": [{ "Action": "UPSERT", "ResourceRecordSet": {"Name": "redwood.example.com","Type": "A","SetIdentifier": "region-eu-west-1","Weight": 60, "TTL": 60, "ResourceRecords": [{"Value": "54.12.34.56"}]}}]}'
- GCP example for DNS: gcloud dns record-sets transaction start; add/replace with lower weight; execute.

When to promote warm-standby (escalation):
- After 15 minutes of mitigations with no >50% reduction in error/latency AND evidence of region control-plane or peering-level issues.
- Warm-standby promotion checklist:
  1) Verify standby has current model artifacts, container images, and infra templates.
  2) Confirm KV cache priming path: for cracking cold-start latency we will run a targeted synthetic replay (see section below) to warm model KV caches and embeddings caches.
  3) Change DNS TTLs to 60s (if not already) and start progressive weight shift in DNS/Global LB over 3 steps: 25% -> 60% -> 100% over 20 minutes with health-check gating.
  4) Coordinate with networking to announce any BGP prefixes if needed (rare; prefer DNS weight shift).

KV / cache warming recipe (important for inference latency):
- Do not cut traffic cold to standby. Use a controlled synthetic warmup: run the last 5k unique prompts + 2 variants each targeting top-10 heavy routes. Prioritize prefix/KV caches and model kv-cache priming to avoid initial token-generation spikes.
- Commands: k8s job: kubectl apply -f warmup-job.yaml --namespace=standby-inference
- Monitor model_latency_kv_hit_ratio and model_inference_p50. Aim for KV hit ratio > 60% before final weight step.

Rollback criteria (abandon and revert):
- If after final cutover error rate climbs >20% above pre-incident baseline in new primary region for more than 10 minutes, start immediate rollback to prior region config and notify execs.
- If network anomalies observed (BGP flaps, provider degraded) then revert DNS weights and open ticket with provider.

Observability checklist during execution:
- Open a dedicated incident dashboard with time-series: global_request_rate, region_request_rate, region_error_rate, model_latency_p95, kv_cache_hit_ratio, lb_connection_errors, infra_autoscale_events. Share link in incident channel.
- Enable expanded tracing sampling for affected routes for at least 1 hour.

Operator hints and gotchas (lessons learned):
- TTLs matter: if public DNS TTL is > 300s we cannot rely on rapid cutover. If we have to make emergency changes and TTL is high, simultaneously alert CDN edge teams to invalidate or adjust origin behavior.
- Provider DNS consoles sometimes show a "pending" change state for a few seconds even after API success — do not panic unless > 30s.
- Promoting standby without warming KV caches yields a poor UX (high p95) even if requests succeed; include a cache-warm gating check.
- Anycast/BGP approaches cutover faster but are harder to scope — reserve them for full-region evacuations only.

Post-incident tasks (within 48h):
- Run a postmortem doc template (link: https://confluence.redwood.com/infra/incident-retro-template) and populate timeline, root cause hypothesis, and contributing factors.
- Update this playbook with any command changes and attach the exact Route53/CloudDNS change-batches used.
- Add synthetic warmup jobs to the standby pipeline so future promotions happen with automated priming.
- Add a scheduled drill to exercise the weight-shift path (quarterly).

Open questions / TODOs for SRE team:
- Can we automate a "pre-warm and verify" step in our deployment pipeline so that warm-standby is always within 5% of production latency? (owner: deployments)
- Do we want a runbook variant that uses BGP anycast pre-announce for <2 minute cutover (owner: networking)?
- Should we add per-customer sticky-routing exemption during partial region issues for high-value customers (owner: platform)?

Appendix A — small checklist for on-call to read fast:
- Step 0: Confirm alert scope (dig + traceroute)
- Step 1: Reduce region weight by 20% and watch for 2 min
- Step 2: If no improvement, run KV warmup against standby and start staged DNS weight shift
- Step 3: If final cutover fails, rollback and open provider support ticket

Appendix B — example quick commands (copy/paste friendly):
- Check DNS from multiple vantage points:
  dig +short @8.8.8.8 redwood.example.com ; dig +short @1.1.1.1 redwood.example.com
- Traceroute (example): traceroute -n -w 2 -q 1 <edge-ip>
- Start synthetic warmup job (k8s): kubectl create job warmup-standby-$(date +%s) --image=registry.redwood/standby-warmup:stable -- /bin/warmup --batch-file /tmp/warm_prompts.json

Notes to self (informal):
- Consider automating weight shifts for short-lived spikes (5–10m) with a circuit-breaker so operators don't have to babysit.
- Keep the warm-standby images no older than 24h behind production to minimize drift.

End of draft. Please add comments inline or push changes to the runbook branch.
